body: A woman is at her kitchen table on a Thursday evening with a builder’s quote in front of her and a biro she keeps clicking. The price is fine. The price was never the thing. She is going down the sheet looking for one sentence — the one he said on the phone three weeks ago about what happens if the damp comes back through the new plaster, which he said twice, easily, and which she believed. It is not on the page. Everything else is, itemised, VAT and all. She reads it again in case she went past it. Then she puts the biro down and does not sign anything that evening.

He was not lying to her on the phone. He probably meant every word and would probably honour it. But a thing that is only in somebody’s intention is a different object from a thing that is written on a page, and she has been alive long enough to know which one survives a bad winter.
Any ministry using these tools should be able to say plainly where its line is. Here is ours, written down so that it can be checked rather than merely trusted.

Doctrine is not generated. What this band teaches is set by people, and it does not move because a model produced a pleasing sentence. Scripture is chosen, not suggested — the passage a song stands on is selected by someone who read it in context, and read what comes before and after it. And no pastoral claim is invented: a station may encourage, and it may hand a listener the Word, but it will not tell them what Yahuah is saying to them specifically. That is not a job to automate. On reflection it is not really a job to broadcast either.

That last one is the strictest of the three and it is the one that costs. Across all 121 frequencies on this band, no station will ever tell you that God has a particular word for you this morning, and no host on any of them will produce one on request.

It costs because that is precisely what people most want, and what a model is best at supplying. Ask any of these systems what God is saying to you and it will hand back something warm, specific and delivered with total confidence, because fluency is what the technology has and doubt is what it lacks. The temptation is not theoretical. It is the easiest way to make any of this feel powerful, and refusing it means accepting that some listeners will find this band cooler than the alternative on the day they most needed heat. A boundary nobody wrote down is not a boundary. It is an intention, and intentions drift quietly under deadline.

That word, deadline, is doing real work. Nobody abandons a principle in a meeting where the principle is on the agenda. It goes at half past six on a Friday, when a frequency is due to open on Monday, the person who would have objected is on leave, and the shortcut is so small that arguing about it would look precious. That is how every standard in every industry has eroded, and it is why the standard has to live somewhere outside the memory of whoever happens to be tired that evening.

So the work is split, and the split is the whole architecture. What the tools do sits entirely downstream of the decisions above. They compose, they voice, they illustrate, they translate, they schedule. That is craft, and craft is exactly the sort of thing it is reasonable to get help with — nobody has ever thought less of a hymn because the organist was reading printed music somebody else engraved. Authority is not craft, and it does not travel downstream with the rest.
The distinction is easier to see than to state. So take a case.

Consider the strongest argument on the other side, because there is one. A model can read the whole of Scripture in a way no person can hold in their head at once, find the passage that speaks to a described situation, and phrase it better at four in the morning than a tired human being would. Why not let it? The answer is not that it would get the verse wrong. It would very often get the verse right. The answer is that the step from here is the passage to here is what it means about your marriage is not retrieval at all. It is an act of pastoral authority, taken by someone who will still be there next month, who knows what you did not say, and who can be wrong in front of you and answer for it. No version of a model can be answerable.
Authority has to belong to someone who can be held to it.

A woman of twenty-six cannot sleep and it is twenty to two. Six months ago she did something she has told nobody about, and it has settled into the part of the night where there is nothing else to look at. She picks up her phone and types the question — whether she is forgiven — into the first thing that will answer it, because there is no one else awake. What comes back is warm, well constructed and entirely reassuring, and she reads it three times and feels better, genuinely better, for about a day and a half. Then it is two in the morning again and she notices she cannot remember who told her.

Nothing false was said to her. That is the uncomfortable part. She was handed a true sentence by something that could not stand behind it, and a sentence nobody stands behind will not hold weight at two in the morning twice.

Publishing a list like this has a real cost, and it is not embarrassment. A written boundary makes a ministry slower and occasionally worse. Some listener will ask a direct question and be handed the Word and a suggestion to talk to their pastor instead of the personal answer they wanted, and they will find that cold. Some will go and get a warmer answer somewhere that has no such list, in fourteen seconds. That is a genuine loss of people and it will not be argued away here.

But a boundary that cost nothing would not be a boundary; it would be a description of what we did not happen to want to do. The point of writing it down is precisely that it binds us on the day it is expensive, and the days it is expensive are the only days it matters. The builder who puts the damp clause in the quote is worse off than the builder who says it on the phone. That is why the clause is worth something, and it is exactly why she was reading the sheet instead of remembering the conversation.

So the reason to publish a list like this rather than simply keep to it is that a boundary nobody wrote down is not a boundary. Written down, it can be pointed at, including by you. If you ever hear a station on this dial tell a listener what God is saying to them personally, or watch doctrine here move because a machine phrased something well, that is not a disappointment to absorb quietly. It is a breach of something published, and you are entitled to say so in those words.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial and it helps to know they are there. There is music, which is most of the band — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. The list above applies identically to every one of them, which is the only way a list of this kind is worth anything.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 306.20 — Hebraic Celebrations. It is Messianic and Hebraic worship built around the feast days, and it is the clearest illustration on the band of what this article has been arguing, because its calendar is not ours. Nobody here decides when those days fall. They were fixed a very long time ago, by someone else, and the station simply follows them round the year whether or not the timing is convenient for programming. That is what an external authority looks like when it is actually operating rather than being professed: a schedule somebody would like to move and cannot.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than a policy notice, though it is both. Put HM 306.20 on this week and listen the way that woman read the quote — not for the warm parts, but for whether what was said on the phone is actually on the page. Hold it against the list. If it holds, that is worth more to you than any assurance in this article. And if it ever stops holding, you will have the sentence in front of you, in writing, which is the entire reason it was written down.
